prop: Every observation in this design was taken against the tetel worktree at commit 043ecb041f02a0d74b90876641eaa573d73a2738 (branch main).

`brief::build` today performs no filtering — it maps each `Claim` to a `BriefItem` one-for-one — and its doc comment forbids dropping a claim from the brief on account of what its evidence ledger already holds, so any owed-scheduling surface that removed claims from `build`'s output would contradict an invariant already stated in the code.

`brief::build` takes `&[Claim]` and nothing else, so owed-ness — which depends on evidence records — cannot be computed inside `build` as it is currently shaped; the owed list must be computed by a caller that also holds the memo's evidence records.

Owed rules 1 and 2 can be taken directly from `analyze_ledger`'s existing outputs — rule 1 is membership in `ungrounded_claims` (no evidence record at all for the claim id) and rule 2 is membership in `out_of_proof` (records exist, all with a digest differing from `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`) — with no new predicate over records needed for either.

`analyze_ledger` already holds two different record sets for one claim — `fresh` (digest exactly equals the current proposition digest) and `grading_current` (digest empty OR equal), the latter grandfathering pre-digest records — so the confirmation floor must name which set it counts; counting `grading_current` would let a record that predates the digest field discharge the floor, which under-schedules, whereas counting `fresh` errs toward scheduling.

Every evidence record already stores the pin it was graded against, in `EvidenceRecord::pin`, a field carried for fidelity that no check currently reads; so pin-change detection can be implemented by comparing a record's `pin` against the claim's current `pin`, and that comparison is answerable on ledgers written before the change, whereas folding the pin into the digest would alter every claim's current digest and drive every existing record into `out_of_proof` at once.

The ticket's premise for rule 3 — that a claim's pin can change only through a `claim --revise` that alters `--cites` — is false: a claim's pin is not derived from its cited facts at all, but parsed by `find_stated_pin` from a document-level "at pin `<hash>`" sentence in the prose between the nearest preceding heading and the ledger table, and the one parsed value is assigned to every claim in that table.

Because one parsed pin is assigned to every claim under a ledger table, a pin change is a document-level event: rule 3 either fires for every claim in the table or for none of it, so it is a re-pin detector for the memo rather than a per-claim scheduling condition.

Every evidence record already stores a pin — on the witnessed path the pin of the grounder's own fact, i.e. the tree it stood in, written expressly so that "was this claim graded against the same tree the memo was written against?" becomes measurable — in a field no check reads today; so rule 3 is implementable as a comparison of that stored pin against the claim's currently stated pin, answerable on ledgers already written, whereas folding the pin into `sha256_hex` would change every pinned claim's current digest and drive every previously written record into `out_of_proof`.
why: F6 shows the record's pin is the grounder's fact pin (witnessed path) or a caller-supplied optional (ingested path), not "the claim's pin at grading time" as C6's original wording implied; the Predicate::pin doc states the exact question it was written for, which is the one rule 3 asks.

prop: Rule 4's "distinct non-author workspaces" count already exists inside `grounding_provenance` as `by_others` — deduped `pass` values of the claim's witnessed records, minus the authoring workspace read from the snapshot's identity — so the floor needs no new notion of workspace identity; it needs that same count restricted to records whose `proposition_digest` matches the current wording, a restriction `grounding_provenance` does not currently apply.

When the memo's snapshot is absent or carries no `identity.json` — `AuthoringIdentity::NoSnapshot` or `SnapshotWithoutIdentity`, the two cases in which `grounding_provenance` already says the author/grounder distinction "cannot be determined from here" — the confirmation floor is not computable, so `brief --owed` must in those states hold every claim owed under rule 4 rather than counting passes it cannot attribute; this is a format-level condition (the file is present and parses, or it is not) and not a heuristic.

All four inputs the owed predicate needs — the claims and their pins, the evidence records, the authoring workspace identity, and the current proposition digests — are already derived from the memo path alone by `check`'s driver in `lib.rs`, which reaches no workspace except the snapshot shipped beside the memo; so `brief --owed` is computable by a grounder given only a memo path, and the surface does not require the author to hand anything over.

Rule 5's matching rule should be the crate's existing `citation_ids_in` rather than a new `C\d+` scan: the existing matcher is already the definition of a row→row citation edge for the dependency-cascade check, it is id-shape-agnostic (a `C\d+` regex would miss real ids of the `R-ROOT` / `CYC-A` shape the crate's own fixtures use, a genuine false-negative class), and its documented error direction is false positives only — which for scheduling means extra grading, never silent under-grading.

Reusing `citation_ids_in` leaves one residual false negative — a proposition that names another claim in unbracketed prose, since `scan_line` begins an id scan only at a `[` byte — and this design states that as a bound rather than widening the matcher, because widening would create a second, disagreeing definition of the same citation edge for a check that already owns one.

Rule 5's fixpoint is a traversal of the reverse citation graph seeded with the claims owed by rules 1-4, and it terminates on any input — including a citation cycle — by the same `visited`-set construction check 5 already uses for row→row cascades; but the graph must be built over ledger claims, which check 5's `row_citers` deliberately excludes, so the construction is reused while the index itself is new.

The confirmation floor and the designer's "stop after the first round that provokes no revision" rule do not conflict, because no rule in that stopping section makes the emptiness of any list a termination condition — the loop stops on machine-clean plus no refuted or unexplained claim, and the round-count rule keys on revisions provoked — so an owed list that is still non-empty at the stopping round is a schedule the run declines to spend another pass on, not an unmet exit criterion.

There should be no `--owed` flag: because the full brief is emitted either way, an owed section is purely additive and there is no prior behaviour a flag would preserve, while TET-46's stated objection to a flag — that it "leaves no trace in what the caller named, only in how they configured the call" — applies with more force to a brief, the one artifact independence rests on, since two passes running `brief` on the same memo would otherwise receive different documents; the confirmation floor stays a parameter, and the value in force is printed in the brief so that this piece of configuration does leave a trace in the artifact.

Rule 4's visibility requirement is met by extending the existing per-claim provenance line in `grounding_provenance` with the number of distinct non-author workspaces that graded the claim's current wording, printed as a bullet in the human-owed partition exactly as that line already is; `check` states the count and never compares it against a floor, because the floor is `brief`'s parameter and a comparison printed by `check` would be a per-claim verdict on a policy setting rather than a count of records.

Extending the per-claim provenance line reaches exactly three files: `grounding_provenance` is named only in src/checks.rs (its field, its zero-init, its definition), src/lib.rs (its single call site) and src/report.rs (the loop printing its strings), with no test or fixture depending on its wording, so the change has one producer and one consumer.

The three symbols this design tells an implementer to touch are bounded by census: `owed_claims` occurs nowhere in the worktree and is green field; `render_text` has exactly one production call site (src/lib.rs:214) and one unit test besides its definition; `grounding_provenance` has one call site and one printer. No part of this design requires modifying `BriefItem`, whose three-field shape is what withholds scope from a grounding pass.

The donor's self-citation exclusion is not needed at the destination: check 5 skips a self-edge so that a root is "never reported as its own dependent", whereas the owed closure's output is a set of ids to grade that already contains its own seeds, so a self-edge can only re-derive owed-ness a claim already has and changes neither the set nor its termination.

The donor's exclusion of ledger claims rests on two properties the owed closure does not share — a ledger claim "cannot be a cascade root (no typed `Status`)" and is not a `Row`, so cannot be a row→row dependent — whereas the owed closure roots at owed-ness under rules 1-4, which is defined for a ledger claim and for nothing else, and its dependents are ledger claims by construction; so the exclusion does not carry across, and the index is built over precisely the population the donor omitted.

The ticket's measurement of TET-30's ledger reproduces exactly on an independent replay: 125 records over 35 distinct (claim, digest) pairs, 90 repeats of which 56 are same-workspace and 34 cross-workspace, 7 of those 34 giving a verdict no earlier workspace had given, every one of them `supports` to `qualifies`, at ordinals 5/1/1 for the 2nd/3rd/4th grading workspace.

On the same replay, a rule with no confirmation floor — one workspace-grading per wording — would have retained none of the seven discoveries while cutting workspace-gradings from 69 to 35; N=2 retains five of seven at 51 gradings (a 26% reduction, slightly less than the ticket's estimated 28%), N=3 retains six at 60, and N=4 retains all seven at 67. The floor is therefore what carries the discovery property, and the saving is bought against it monotonically.

The owed predicate as decided here: a claim is owed iff it is in `analyze_ledger`'s `ungrounded_claims`, or in its `out_of_proof`, or the pin stored on its records differs from the memo's currently stated pin, or fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have a record whose `proposition_digest` equals the current proposition's, or `citation_ids_in` finds in its proposition text the id of a claim that is itself owed — the last computed to a fixpoint. Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot, and each of the first four reuses a set the crate already computes.

Of the four pieces the ticket requires to ship together, only the confirmation floor's necessity is measured here — the replay shows the rule without it retains none of the seven findings; the necessity of pin detection, the closure and the visibility line is argued from the code in this memo and is not measured by anything, and this design does not extend the floor's evidence to cover them.

The textual closure needs no author-side claim-to-claim dependency edge: its edges are read out of proposition text by `citation_ids_in` at schedule time, from artifacts the memo carries, so grounding scheduling is computable without the re-evaluation obligation the ticket puts out of scope.

When the memo's snapshot is absent or carries no `identity.json` — `AuthoringIdentity::NoSnapshot` or `SnapshotWithoutIdentity`, the two cases in which `grounding_provenance` already says the author/grounder distinction "cannot be determined from here" — the confirmation floor is not computable, so the brief's owed list must in those states hold every claim owed under rule 4 rather than counting passes it cannot attribute; this is a format-level condition (the file is present and parses, or it is not) and not a heuristic.
why: C16 decides the owed list is unconditional rather than a `--owed` flag; this claim's wording named it as a flag and would now contradict that decision.

prop: No tree-identity operand can serve as an owed condition at all. A world-state marker hashes HEAD together with the working-tree delta, so it changes on every commit and on any uncommitted edit to a tracked file, and a state fixed at authoring time cannot be re-observed by a later pass short of restoring both; the authoring markers are frozen in immutable facts, so re-rendering carries them forward unchanged. An owed condition keyed on tree identity therefore schedules work that no pass can discharge — the "red nobody can clear" that `analyze_ledger`'s own comments name as the defect that forced its stale-record partition to be rebuilt. The ticket's pin defect is real but its remedy is a report, not a schedule: carrying the predicate's `world` markers into `EvidenceRecord` — one field at read-back, in a type whose 22 occurrences span two modules — lets `check` say which tree each grading pass stood in beside the tree the memo's own facts were taken against, as a human-owed line that never fails the run. prop: The ticket's pin defect is real but its remedy is a report, not a schedule: carrying the predicate's `world` markers into `EvidenceRecord` — one field at read-back, in a type whose occurrences fall on 22 lines across two modules — lets `check` say which tree each grading pass stood in beside the tree the memo's own facts were taken against, as a human-owed line that never fails the run. That is the disposition an observation deserves when it is true, worth a reader's judgement, and permanently unclearable.
why: Same correction as C19: the census counts lines, not matches, so "22 occurrences" named the wrong unit.

prop: A tree-identity operand is dischargeable exactly while the repository still stands where the memo's facts were taken: a marker is a deterministic function of HEAD and the working-tree delta, and recomputing it at the pinned commit with a clean tree reproduces this memo's own facts' marker byte for byte. It stops being dischargeable at the next commit, permanently, because the authoring markers are frozen in immutable facts and re-rendering carries them forward — which is the state four of the five memos in this repository are already in. So rule 3 is not in the owed predicate: an owed condition that is satisfiable only until the next commit and unsatisfiable forever after is not a schedule, and the crate's own comments name a red nobody can clear as the defect that forced its stale-record partition to be rebuilt.
why: Refuted by an attack pass and confirmed by F24: a marker IS reproducible by a later pass at the same clean commit, so the universal "no pass can discharge" was false. The disposition is unchanged but its ground is now the conditional the evidence actually supports.

prop: Whether tree identity should instead be a schedulable condition is not decided by the evidence gathered here, and this design stops rather than choosing a third time. One direction is blocked by the observation that four of five memos in this repository already carry authoring markers no present-day pass can reproduce; the other by the observation that a marker at the pinned commit with a clean tree reproduces exactly, so the rule does work for a memo being actively worked on. The observation that would discriminate is one nobody here can make: how long a memo's grounding rounds run relative to commits landing on its worktree, across more designs than this repository contains.

The closure must not match by citation shape. Across all five rendered memos — 90 claims — not one proposition contains a bracketed citation-shaped id, so a closure built on `citation_ids_in` yields the empty edge set on every memo in the corpus while real unbracketed inter-claim references exist in two of them, including this memo's own C4 naming C5. The matcher is instead membership in the document's own ledger: a whitespace- or punctuation-delimited token in a proposition is an edge when it is byte-equal to an id that this document's ledger defines and is not the claim's own id. That is decidable, needs no shape heuristic, and cannot invent an edge to something that does not exist, because the id set it matches against is the ledger's.
why: Refuted in effect by an attack pass and confirmed by F24: reusing the citation matcher makes disjunct 4 inert on every memo that exists, which is the same "no operand anywhere it would run" standard this design used to kill rule 3. Matching against the ledger's own defined ids removes both the inertness and the false-positive worry that motivated shape matching.

prop: Matching against the ledger's own ids errs toward false positives, which is the safe direction for a schedule: a proposition that mentions a sibling id without depending on it schedules one extra grading and settles nothing. The residual false negative is narrow and stated rather than closed — a proposition that refers to another claim without naming its id, by description rather than reference, is not an edge and cannot be made one without reading prose for meaning. This is a different bound from the one the crate's citation matcher carries, and deliberately so: the citation check asks whether a document cites an id, which is a question about shape, while the closure asks whether a proposition names a claim of this ledger, which is a question about a known set.
why: C12 now matches ledger ids rather than citation shape, so the residual C13 described — an unbracketed reference — is exactly the case now caught, and the real remaining gap is a reference that names no id at all.

prop: The owed predicate as decided here has four disjuncts, not the ticket's five: a claim is owed iff it is in `analyze_ledger`'s `ungrounded_claims`, or in its `out_of_proof`, or fewer than N distinct non-author workspaces have a WITNESSED record whose `proposition_digest` equals the current proposition's, or its proposition names, by an id this document's ledger defines, a claim that is itself owed — the last computed to a fixpoint. The ticket's pin rule is dropped. "Witnessed" is load-bearing in the third, though for a narrower reason than independence: on the witnessed path the pass is a workspace that captured its own facts, whereas an ingested record's `pass` is free text its reporter typed, so counting ingested passes would let a floor be discharged by naming alone. Every disjunct is decidable from the memo, its evidence file and its snapshot; the first two are `analyze_ledger`'s own outputs, but the third needs the digest-matched record set that today is a local inside `analyze_ledger` to be exposed rather than recomputed, so that the crate keeps one definition of "graded on this wording".
why: Two findings from an attack pass: disjunct 4 must match ledger ids rather than `citation_ids_in` (C12, F24), and "witnessed" was spent as an independence guarantee it does not provide — F25 shows a workspace identity certifies a distinct capture effort under a caller-chosen name, not a distinct reader.

prop: The floor counts distinct capture efforts, not distinct readers, and the design should say so rather than lean on the stronger reading. A workspace identity is minted on first use of a caller-chosen name and never rewritten, and the crate defines an independent grounding pass as simply a fresh workspace; what a distinct witnessed `pass` certifies is that separate grounds were captured under a separate identity, not that a separate mind read the claim. That is the property the confirmation floor actually enforces, and it is weaker than independence while still being exactly what the replay measured, since the discoveries there arrived from workspaces that did capture their own grounds.

The replay's empirical content is the ordinal distribution and the cost curve, not the headline that a floor of 1 retains nothing — that figure is entailed by the definition of a discovery as a verdict no earlier workspace gave, whose ordinal is therefore at least 2 on any ledger whatever. What the ledger does show is that seven such verdict changes occurred at all, that five of them arrived from the second workspace to read a wording, and that capping distinct workspaces per wording costs 35, 51, 60 and 67 gradings at N=1 to 4 against 69 unbounded. So N=2 buys five of the seven for sixteen gradings above the dirty-only floor, and each further N buys less.
why: An attack pass showed the N=1-retains-zero figure is true by the definition of "discovery" rather than by anything this ledger does, so it cannot carry the weight the design put on it; the empirical findings that survive are stated instead.

prop: Of the four pieces the ticket requires to ship together, one is measured and three are not. The measurement is the replay's ordinal distribution and cost curve, which say what a floor of 2 buys and at what price; it is not the headline that a floor of 1 finds nothing, which follows from how a discovery is defined. The closure and the visibility line are argued from the code in this memo, nothing measures what their absence would cost, and the fourth, pin-change detection, does not ship as a scheduling rule at all. This design does not extend the measurement's standing to what is only argued.
why: An attack pass observed that the claim named as "the measurement" the one figure that could not have come out otherwise; the proposition now names the part of the replay that carries empirical content.

prop: The projected saving is contingent on pass behaviour that nothing in this design enforces and nothing in this repository can check. A brief emits, per claim, only an id, a proposition, an optional pin and a withheld scope, with no instruction prose in either renderer, and `build`'s own doc requires every claim to stay in the list; so the owed section is an artifact a pass may read and act on, not a mechanism that makes it grade fewer claims. The costs of the feature — threading a floor through two front ends, widening `analyze_ledger`, `grounding_provenance` and `EvidenceRecord` — are unconditional by contrast.

Extending the per-claim provenance line reaches three files by identifier — `grounding_provenance` is named only in src/checks.rs, src/lib.rs's single call site and src/report.rs's printing loop — but the identifier census understates the dependents, because end-to-end tests assert on the strings the function emits rather than on its name: tests/authoring_cli.rs asserts `SELF-GROUNDED` and `cannot be determined from here`, and tests/mcp_cli.rs asserts the absence of the latter. They are substring assertions, so appending a count to a line is likely to leave them passing, but an implementer is told to run them rather than to trust a census by identifier.
why: A grounding pass falsified "no test or fixture depending on its wording" by grepping the emitted strings instead of the symbol; F26 confirms four assertions in two test files. This is the census's own declared blind spot showing up in this design's own reasoning.

prop: Owed rules 1 and 2 can be taken directly from `analyze_ledger`'s existing outputs, with no new predicate over records for either: rule 1 is a claim appearing in `ungrounded_claims`, which is already a `Vec<(String, String)>` of id and proposition and so needs nothing added; rule 2 is a claim appearing in `out_of_proof`, which `analyze_ledger` reports for a claim that has at least one record with a non-empty digest and none whose digest equals `sha256_hex(claim.proposition)`. A claim whose records all carry empty pre-digest digests is in neither set, because both partitions are taken after those records are filtered out — the same grandfathering C5 turns on. Only `out_of_proof` is a list of rendered message strings rather than ids, so only it needs the claim ids reported alongside the messages.
why: A grounding pass found the closing sentence false of `ungrounded_claims`, which is declared as `(id, proposition)` pairs; only `out_of_proof` is message strings.

prop: The textual closure does not ship, and it is deferred on this design's own disposal standard rather than on taste. Its yield is tiny where it can run at all: across the five rendered memos the only inter-claim references inside propositions are three bare tokens naming a sibling id, and no proposition anywhere carries a bracketed one. And no matcher tried here covers both populations the tool serves — the crate's citation scanner finds the bracketed id in the importer's own hand-authored fixture and nothing in the rendered corpus, while a ledger-id token rule finds the rendered corpus's bare references and cannot match a hyphenated id like `X-1` at all, because a hyphen is punctuation. A disjunct carrying a new reverse index and a traversal, to schedule at most three edges in this repository's whole history, is not worth its surface until someone states its yield on a population it works on.

why: Refuted by an attack pass and confirmed by F27: the ledger-id token rule this claim decided on cannot match a hyphenated id, which is the id shape of the imported-ledger population the crate's own fixtures use, so it relocates the inertness it was chosen to remove. C35 defers the closure rather than choosing a third matcher.

Refuted by an attack pass: the residual it called narrow omits an entire class — a by-id reference on any ledger whose ids are hyphenated (F27). It described the bound of a matcher this design no longer chooses.

Refuted by an attack pass: it names `citation_ids_in` as the closure's matcher, which C12 had already rejected and C35 now defers entirely, so it contradicted the design it belonged to. The out-of-scope conclusion it carried is restated in C36 without depending on a matcher.
The closure it specifies a traversal for is deferred by C35, so the claim describes machinery this design no longer asks anyone to build.
It answers a transplant premise for a mechanism this design no longer installs, X1 having been withdrawn with the closure it served.
Same as C20: it answers a premise of the withdrawn transplant X1, whose mechanism the deferred closure was the only destination for.

prop: The exclusion the ticket insists on holds without any claim-to-claim machinery, and holds more simply now that the closure is deferred: every disjunct that ships reads only records against a claim's own id, so grounding scheduling needs no edge between claims at all, and nothing in this design asks an author to re-evaluate a dependent.

why: An attack pass computed the marginal steps and found the diminishing-returns clause false — 9 gradings per discovery at N=2→3 against 7 at N=3→4 — which was the ground the memo gave for its default.

prop: The floor's default is 2, stated rather than left to the call site, and the ground for the value is a trade this design states rather than a diminishing return it does not have. Both front ends today reach `brief_file(path, json)` with no floor argument at all, so a caller who supplies nothing must get a defined value. On the replayed ledger 2 is the only floor at which the feature saves materially — 51 gradings against 69 — while 4 retains every discovery for 67 of 69 and therefore saves almost nothing. Choosing 2 buys an 18-grading saving at the price of two of seven discoveries; a memo whose stakes make that price too high raises N, which is why the value is a parameter.
why: An attack pass observed that the only argument offered for 2 was the definitional N=1 figure, and that nothing argued 2 over 3 or 4; the value is now argued from the cost curve with the discoveries it gives up named.
